questions.question: What happens when `append` has enough capacity or needs more space?
questions.title: How append grows a Go slice
questions.direct_answer: The built-in `append` returns a slice containing the original elements followed by the new ones. When the required length fits within capacity, it reuses the existing backing array. When it does not fit, it uses larger storage and copies the old elements before adding the new values. Because either path can occur, always keep the returned slice. Reuse can make writes visible through another slice sharing the array; reallocation separates the returned slice. Go does not guarantee a particular capacity growth formula.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether both append paths and their aliasing consequences are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming append always mutates in place or always allocates.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Only the returned contents are guaranteed; allocation size and growth factor are implementation details.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `append(s, values...)` returns the slice that represents the completed append.
If the new length fits within `cap(s)`, append reuses the backing array.
If the new length exceeds capacity, append uses larger storage and preserves the old prefix.
Reuse may affect aliases; reallocation leaves aliases attached to the old array.
The resulting elements are guaranteed, but the exact capacity growth rule is not.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The built-in `append` adds one or more values after a slice's current elements and returns the resulting slice. For example, `next := append(current, 30)` gives next one extra element. The returned value matters because a slice carries its own length, capacity, and access to backing storage.

If `len(s) + added <= cap(s)`, the new elements fit in storage already available to the slice. Append writes them immediately after the old length and returns a longer view of the same array. No element copy is needed on this path.

When the required length is greater than capacity, the current array cannot hold the result. Append obtains suitable storage, copies the existing elements, writes the added values, and returns a slice over that storage. The old slice still describes the old array and keeps its old length.

Suppose `a := make([]int, 1, 2)` and `b := append(a, 20)`. They can still share storage, so changing `b[0]` changes `a[0]`. Appending once more to full `b` requires other storage, so later writes through that returned slice no longer reach a.

Go guarantees the order and values in the returned slice, not whether storage is reused or how much capacity a new allocation receives. Always assign or return the result of `append`, and use explicit copying when an API requires independent data rather than relying on an allocation side effect.

sections.title: How append chooses a destination
sections.content:
Appending starts with a simple requirement: the result needs room for the current length plus every added value. The operation always returns a slice whose visible elements are the old prefix followed by the new values. What changes is where those elements live.

When the required length fits within capacity, the backing array already has enough reserved positions. Append can place the new values after the old length and return another slice view over that array. Existing slices keep their own lengths, but a longer alias may already expose the positions being written. This is why reuse can have visible side effects.

When the required length exceeds capacity, append must use other storage. It copies the existing prefix, adds the new values, and returns a descriptor for that storage. Any aliases remain connected to the old array. The result is correct on both paths only when the caller keeps the returned descriptor with `s = append(s, value)` or passes it onward.

The runtime is free to choose a suitable new capacity. Its growth policy may vary with Go version, element size, and current capacity. Preallocation can reduce expected allocations, but program correctness must depend on the returned elements and explicit ownership rules, never on a guessed growth factor.

sections.title: The two storage paths through append
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[append s with k values] --> B{len s plus k fits in cap s?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Reuse available backing-array positions]
  B -->|No| D[Use larger storage and copy old prefix]
  C --> E[Return slice with new length]
  D --> E
```
Both paths return the same logical sequence; only the storage relationship differs.

sections.title: Observe one reuse and one reallocation
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := make([]int, 1, 2)
	a[0] = 10
	b := append(a, 20)
	b[0] = 11
	fmt.Println("after reuse:", a, b)

	c := append(b, 30)
	c[0] = 99
	fmt.Println("after growth:", b, c)
}
```

questions.question: Why must you assign the result of `append` in Go?
questions.title: Why Go append returns a slice
questions.direct_answer: You must assign or return the result of `append` because a slice variable is a value with its own length, capacity, and backing-storage reference. Append computes a new slice value whose length includes the added elements, and it may also point to different storage. It does not replace the caller's variable automatically. Use `s = append(s, value)` in the same scope, or have a helper return the updated slice. Direct element assignment is different because it writes through an existing slice without changing its descriptor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether slice descriptor changes are distinguished from element changes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Appending in a helper without returning and assigning the resulting slice.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Return the slice whenever a function may change its length or capacity.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A slice variable keeps its own length, capacity, and backing-storage reference.
`append` returns a descriptor whose length includes the new elements.
The normal pattern is `s = append(s, value)`.
A helper that may append should return the updated slice to its caller.
Element writes can be shared, but length and capacity changes stay in the returned value.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A slice variable is a value that records a visible length, a capacity, and access to backing storage. Passing it to a function copies that value. The function can still reach shared elements, but it cannot silently replace the caller's slice variable with a longer descriptor.

The expression `append(s, value)` returns a slice whose length includes value. It may reuse s's array or use another one, but either way the length change exists in the result. The original variable keeps the descriptor it had before the call.

In one scope, write `s = append(s, value)`. This works for both storage paths: s receives the longer length when the array is reused and receives the new storage reference when growth required another array.

A helper normally has a shape such as `func add(s []int, v int) []int { return append(s, v) }`. The caller then writes `s = add(s, v)`. If the helper discards its local result, the caller cannot see the new length and may not be able to reach reallocated storage at all.

An assignment such as `s[0] = 9` changes an existing backing-array element, so aliases may observe it without a returned slice. Append can change length, capacity, and storage. Those descriptor changes must be returned to the variable that should own the resulting logical slice.

sections.title: Why the caller's length does not change by itself
sections.content:
A slice is passed to a function by value, just like other Go values. The copied descriptor may lead to the same array, which is why a function can change an existing element and the caller can observe it. The caller and callee still have separate descriptor variables, including separate length and capacity fields.

Append creates a descriptor for a longer visible range. If capacity is available, the new element may be written into shared backing storage, but it sits beyond the caller's unchanged length. The caller cannot index that position through its old slice. If capacity is not available, the returned descriptor is also the only one that reaches the new array.

The assignment `s = append(s, value)` handles both cases without needing to know which happened. Across a function boundary, return the updated slice and let the caller assign it. A helper that appends locally and returns nothing can appear to work while inspecting the shared array, yet its caller still has the old logical collection.

This rule applies to any helper that may alter slice length or capacity. A function that only changes existing elements does not need to return the slice for that mutation to be visible, although returning a value may still make an API clearer. The key distinction is array content versus the descriptor that defines the visible collection.

sections.title: The returned descriptor must reach the caller
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Caller slice - len 2] --> B[Helper receives descriptor copy]
  B --> C[append returns local result - len 3]
  C -->|Discard result| D[Caller remains len 2]
  C -->|Return and assign| E[Caller becomes len 3]
```
Backing storage may be reused or replaced; the new length reaches the caller only through the returned slice.

questions.question: Can appending to one slice change another slice?
questions.title: Append, spare capacity, and slice aliasing
questions.direct_answer: Yes. Appending to one slice can change values seen through another slice when both views share a backing array and the append reuses spare capacity. Append writes new elements immediately after its input slice's current length; those array positions may already be visible through a longer alias. If capacity is exhausted, the returned slice uses other storage and the old alias is unchanged. A full slice expression can prevent reuse beyond a boundary, while `slices.Clone` or `copy` gives independent element storage.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether append writes are traced against all live slice views.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Looking only at slice lengths and forgetting shared capacity behind them.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use an explicit copy when preserving the source is part of the contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Two slice values can expose different ranges of the same backing array.
Append writes after the input slice's length, not after every alias's length.
Within capacity, that write may replace a value visible through a longer alias.
Beyond capacity, the returned slice grows on different storage.
Use a capacity fence for append isolation or a clone for independent elements.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Appending can affect another slice only when their visible ranges come from the same backing array and the append reuses that array. Each slice has its own length, but length does not create a storage boundary between aliases.

Take `all := []int{10, 20, 30, 40}` and `head := all[:2]`. Head has length two and capacity four. The call `append(head, 99)` reuses the array and writes 99 at backing index two, which is also `all[2]`.

After that append, all still has length four but now contains `[10, 20, 99, 40]`. The returned head has length three. Append did not expand all; both descriptors simply observe an array position that was overwritten through the shorter view.

The expression `protected := all[:2:2]` gives the view capacity two. Its next append must use other storage, so it cannot consume all's third position. Current elements still alias all, because a full slice expression limits growth but does not copy them.

Use shared capacity when in-place cooperation is intentional. Use a full slice expression when existing elements may remain shared but appended elements must not overwrite adjacent source data. Use `slices.Clone` or `copy` when even current-element assignments must be independent.

sections.title: Why a shorter slice can overwrite a longer view
sections.content:
A slice's length tells append where its new values begin. It does not describe every live view of the same array. A shorter slice can therefore treat a backing-array position as spare capacity while a longer alias already treats that position as an existing element.

For `all := []int{10, 20, 30, 40}` and `head := all[:2]`, both slices start at the same array position. Head sees only the first two values, but its capacity reaches the end of all's array. Appending 99 to head can reuse backing index two. The returned slice correctly contains three elements, while all observes its former value 30 replaced by 99. Their lengths stay independent even though the storage write is shared.

If head has no spare capacity, append must return a slice using other storage and all keeps its values. Code can deliberately create this condition with `head := all[:2:2]`. That full slice expression prevents append from reusing positions after head's visible range, but assignments such as `head[0] = 7` still change all because current elements were not copied.

Choose the boundary explicitly. Capacity limiting protects adjacent source positions from future growth. Cloning protects the current elements as well, although a slice of pointers is still only shallow-copied. Relying on append to happen to allocate makes ownership change when capacity changes and is therefore fragile.

sections.title: What an existing alias observes after append
sections.content:
| Starting relationship | Append storage path | Effect on the existing alias |
|---|---|---|
| Shared array with spare capacity | Reuse the array | Overlapping positions may change |
| Shared array with capacity exhausted | Use other storage | Alias keeps the old array values |
| Full slice with `cap == len` | First growth uses other storage | Adjacent source positions are protected |
| Clone before append | Grow independent storage | Clone and source element assignments are separate |

sections.title: Compare shared append with a capacity-fenced append
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	all := []int{10, 20, 30, 40}
	head := all[:2]
	grown := append(head, 99)
	fmt.Println("shared growth:", grown, all)

	source := []int{10, 20, 30, 40}
	fenced := source[:2:2]
	isolated := append(fenced, 99)
	fmt.Println("fenced growth:", isolated, source)
}
```

questions.question: Should you preallocate a slice with length or capacity?
questions.title: Preallocating Go slices with the right length and capacity
questions.direct_answer: Preallocate with length when that many result elements already logically exist and the code will fill them by index: `make([]T, n)` creates n zero-valued, indexable elements. Preallocate only capacity when the result starts empty and grows with append: `make([]T, 0, n)` has length zero and capacity n. Using length n and then appending n values produces 2n elements with unwanted zero values first. Treat capacity as an allocation estimate; reserving too much can waste or retain memory.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether logical length and allocation capacity are chosen independently.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `make([]T, n)` before appending and producing `n` unwanted zero values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reserve only when an estimate is useful; capacity does not belong to the API result.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `make([]T, n)` creates n logical elements that can be filled by index.
`make([]T, 0, n)` creates an empty result with capacity n for append.
Known-size transformations usually need length; filters and collectors usually need capacity.
Allocating length and then appending adds after the zero-valued prefix.
Capacity is an optimization estimate, and excessive reservation can retain memory.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The length in `make([]T, length, capacity)` is part of the collection's current meaning. Those positions already exist, are indexable, and contain T's zero value. Capacity is backing space the slice may use as it grows; it does not add logical elements by itself.

When every input produces exactly one output, allocate the final length. A square operation can start with `out := make([]int, len(input))` and assign `out[i] = n * n`. Every result position is known to exist, so append is unnecessary.

A filter does not know how many values will pass. It can use `out := make([]int, 0, len(input))`: no output elements exist yet, but the input length is a safe upper-bound capacity. Each passing value is then appended to the logical result.

If code creates `out := make([]int, n)` and then appends n values, append starts after the existing n zero-valued elements. The final length is 2n. The allocation succeeded, but length described data that the program did not intend to keep.

A nil slice is valid for append, so preallocation is not required for correctness. Reserve capacity when a reasonable estimate avoids useful allocations. Underestimating normally costs performance; a large overestimate can reserve or retain more memory than the result needs. Do not expose final capacity as an API guarantee.

sections.title: Choosing the right shape before filling a slice
sections.content:
The arguments to `make` describe two different things. Length is the number of elements in the slice immediately after construction. Those elements are real, indexable, and initialized to the type's zero value. Capacity is the backing space available from the slice's start before append needs more storage.

A transformation with a known one-to-one result can allocate its final length and fill by index. If four input numbers always produce four squares, `make([]int, 4)` matches the logical result from the beginning. It avoids growing the slice and lets each result position be assigned directly.

A filter or collector starts differently because no output element exists until a value qualifies. `make([]int, 0, len(input))` starts empty while reserving a reasonable upper bound. Append adds only accepted values. Creating length first and then appending describes two groups of elements: the unwanted zero-valued prefix and the values added afterward.

Preallocation is optional. A nil slice can be appended to correctly, and underestimating capacity normally means extra allocation rather than wrong output. A large overestimate can hold more memory than needed, especially when a small result remains live for a long time. Choose length from the result's known logical size, choose capacity from a useful estimate, and do not make observed final capacity part of the API contract.

sections.title: Length and capacity fit different construction patterns
sections.content:
| Construction | Initial length | Initial capacity | How to fill it |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `make([]T, n)` | n | n | Assign known result positions by index |
| `make([]T, 0, n)` | 0 | n | Append a result with an estimated upper bound |
| `var out []T` | 0 | 0 | Append a small or unpredictable result without preallocation |
